Name: Landline
Description:
Hey, remember when you could actually call into a show and be part of it? Yeah, before everything turned into scrolling, lurking, and firing off comment-section hot takes? Well, guess what? We're bringing it back. This is Landline, the call-in show you didn’t know you needed—but definitely do.

This isn’t a podcast where you sit quietly while someone drones on for an hour. Nope. This is your chance to jump into the chaos, say your piece, and maybe even make someone laugh so hard they fart. Because, honestly, what else are you doing?

 What You’re Getting Yourself Into:
- Call-In Chaos: Yes, actual calls. No DMs, no emoji reacts—just you, your voice, and whatever story, rant, or random thought you’ve been dying to share.
- Peak Nostalgia Vibes: If you’re longing for the days of call-in radio, public access weirdness, and the kind of raw, unscripted fun that used to rule the airwaves, welcome home.
- Laugh Therapy: Life’s ridiculous, so let’s laugh at it together. We’re talking about the kind of laughs that make you rethink your life choices.

 Why You Should Call In:
Because you can. When’s the last time anyone handed you a microphone and said, “Go ahead, say what's on your mind”? That’s what we’re doing here. It’s your shot to be the caller everyone remembers—or the one they immediate forget. Either way, you win.

 Where to Find Us:
- Public access TV (because we’re fancy like that).
- YouTube (so your mom can watch it later).
- Podcast platforms everywhere (listen while you pretend to work).

So go on, dust off your inner Wayne or Garth and pick up the phone. Let’s make this weird, funny, and maybe even a little meaningful. Or not. That’s up to you.

Located amidst the serene forest landscape of Durham, North Carolina, our journey began in 2014 with the launch of our very first radio station — WDUR 1490 AM, proudly owned and operated by Arohi Media LLC. Broadcasting through our 1,000-watt non-directional tower, we introduced the Triangle’s first 24/7 Desi Radio Network, bringing Hindi news, talk, and Bollywood music to the rapidly growing South Asian and Indian Subcontinent community in the Raleigh-Durham-Chapel Hill-Cary region.
Building on this success, we expanded our reach by leasing the HD-4 Channel of 99.9 WCMC-FM and soon launched our own FM translator on 101.9 FM — followed by 99.9 FM HD-3 Telugu. Today, Radio Nyra proudly broadcasts across multiple frequencies and digital platforms, connecting tens of thousands of listeners every week.
From Bollywood beats to community talk shows, immigration news to business insights, we bridge the gap between home and homeland — delivering content that informs, entertains, and inspires.
Beyond radio, Arohi Media LLC also provides comprehensive social media marketing and digital advertising solutions, helping brands reach the vibrant Indian and South Asian audiences across North Carolina and the United States. Our integrated marketing approach — combining on-air promotions, podcasting, events, and social media campaigns — ensures unmatched visibility and engagement for every client.
Whether it’s through 99.9 FM HD-3 Telugu, 99.9 FM HD-4 Hindi, 101.9 FM, or 1490 AM, Radio Nyra continues to be the voice of the community — a trusted platform where cultures connect and conversations thrive.

Name: The Bum Diary
Description:
the bum diary, for all good reason or purpose, is a symptom of our trying times... when the world seemed most destined to spiral out and vanish, it arrived. not as any sort of savior or hero, but as an observational force. bum diary is a reflection of all the ugliness and beauty it is graced with witnessing, regurgitating back out a rundown of the events that puts the mess back together in one comprehensible piece. sometimes there’s nothing legible enough to comprehend in one of our stories... but there’s truth to find in the attempt at making it that way. 

the bum diary’ is the name-child of Hunter. S Thompson’s 1998 novel — which was actually written in the 1960’s — Rum Diary. The book loosely follows a journalist, Paul Kemp, and his unusual journey through Puerto Rico on a reporting stint that even he himself can’t see the purpose for. It’s not only the gig, but the journey too, that perplexes him so. Nothing thrilling, rousing or substantial occurs throughout the entire novel, but there’s a certain pointless truth to the whole thing that excited feelings of melancholy and profundities in so many. The pure sensation of regularity that you could only find in the bottom of a rum glass — that is what Bum Diary truly seeks to capture.

With platforms, consumer behaviors, and campaign trends shifting rapidly, it’s harder than ever for academics to keep teaching and researching in ways that feel timely, grounded, and inspiring.

Marketingaroo exists to change that. We translate fast-moving marketing practice into digestible, relevant content for academic use. Whether you're designing a module, updating your slides, prepping for a conference, mentoring PhD students, or exploring a new research angle, we’ve got your back. At the core of the project is the Flavoursome Marketing Digest—a playful but rigorous roundup of campaigns, trends, scandals, and martech developments, paired with reflections and provocations that make it easier to bring practice into the classroom. It's not just about what happened in marketing this week—it’s about why it matters for education and theory.

We also create modular, low-prep teaching tools, research prompts inspired by real-world brand dilemmas, and ready-to-use classroom examples that energize student discussions and help academics feel connected to what’s happening outside the ivory tower. With a tone that’s critical but never cynical, humorous but never shallow, we celebrate what makes marketing such a dynamic, creative, and sometimes absurd field to teach.

Marketingaroo is powered by educators, not algorithms. There are no subscriptions, no paywalls, and no jargon for the sake of it—just timely, usable, practice-informed content made with care. Because marketing education should be relevant, thought-provoking, and just a little bit more fun. Join us. Use what helps. Share what works. Teach better, together.

We keep it simple: the spots worth your time, served up the way we'd tell a friend.

Restaurant profiles come in two flavors: New & Noteworthy for spots just opening and Best of the Best for places that have earned their status. We tell you what to order, who it's perfect for, and yes, even the parking situation. All the stuff we'd want to know as diners.

A Quickie With... features our interviews with Miami's best restaurant personalities. We share hot takes on controversial stuff in Miami's restaurant world that needs to be said. Each week, we do Best Thing I Ate This Week where we each share our favorite dish from the past few days.

And better yet, three times a week, we send out newsletters with Miami restaurant news. The kind of quick updates that keep you in the know without the fluff.

Name: Meaningful Impact
Description:
Through our awards program and podcast, Meaningful Impact recognizes projects which benefit both a company and the greater good.

For example, award-eligible projects include: product marketing that also supports a cause; sustainability initiatives that also reduce costs; advocacy campaigns that also attract new customers; strategic philanthropy which also boosts reputation; as well as employee inclusion and volunteer programs that also boost retention.

In fact, to inspire the greatest good, any kind of corporate responsibility is eligible for a Meaningful Impact Award if the project achieves a win-win... win:
1. a mission win for a cause
2. a financial win for the company
3. a self-fulfillment win for the project-team leaders, personally or professionally

If you're responsible for marketing or PR at your company, or if you help clients manage their reputation, you’ll especially appreciate the publicist-friendly features of the Meaningful Impact Awards.

Unlike annual award competitions which consider nominations just once per year, nominations for Meaningful Impact Awards are typically reviewed within two weeks. So, you can submit an award nomination today and potentially win soon. There’s even an expedited-review option available, if you've got an imperative to announce good news within a few days.

Optional publicity add-ons are also available, making it easy to promote your win via sponsored content at partner publications, such as CSR.org. 

Visit MeaningfulImpact.com/PR for more information on the publicity options.

When you apply for a Meaningful Impact Award, the first step is to select your nominated project and its award recipients.

Nominations are accepted on behalf of:
• individuals
• project teams
• companies
• trade associations

If your nominee does win a Meaningful Impact Award, the recognition will be conferred in one of three award tiers:  Goodwill, Leadership, or Paragon.  

Download the Entry Kit & Success Guide at MeaningfulImpact.com/Kit

Caregiver Bliss was born out of personal experience and a deep understanding of the unique demands and rewards of elderly family caregiving. Our founder, Jennifer Ann, witnessed firsthand the dedication and sacrifices made by family caregivers when caring for their aging parents.

At Caregiver Bliss, our platform offers a wealth of resources to address the diverse needs of caregivers. From practical tips on managing daily caregiving tasks to navigating complex healthcare systems, we strive to equip caregivers with the knowledge they need to make informed decisions and provide the best care possible.

We also deeply understand and appreciate the invaluable role of family caregivers. These remarkable individuals selflessly dedicate their lives to caring for their elderly family members, providing unwavering support in every aspect of their lives. Often, they find themselves juggling countless duties and making significant sacrifices.

At Caregiver Bliss, our mission is to empower and inspire caregivers through education and information. We strive to make a positive difference in the lives of those who selflessly care for others. We firmly believe that by equipping caregivers with the knowledge and resources they need, we can help them find balance, strength, and resilience in their caregiving journey.

Together, we can make a profound impact and improve the lives of caregivers and their loved ones.

Name: The Shorthorn Media
Description:
Years before the “UT” preceded the “A’  at the college now known as the University of Texas at Arlington, and years before there was a Longhorn in the family, there was The Shorthorn. No relation, thanks. 

In 1919, students at what was then known as Grubbs Vocational College needed a name for their fledgling literary/humor magazine. With a $2.50 prize from the dean as incentive, an ensuing contest yielded such poetic possibilities as KornKob, Swat News, Horse Sense, Grubworm and Tool for the name of the new publication. In a three-ballot election runoff, the student body chose Shorthorn over other finalists GVC Shots and Thistle.

The first issue — 6 by 9 inches, 48 pages with a bull in a bull’s-eye for a cover — appeared in April 1919. The first newsroom masqueraded as a wide spot in the hallway leading to the adviser’s office on the third floor of Ransom Hall, the campus' oldest building. 

The Shorthorn evolved into a newspaper in 1921 and has thrived in spite of a world war, the Depression, ice storms and too many technical conversions and computer crashes to count. On a campus noted for change, The Shorthorn has been a constant, growing into a daily publication in 1977 after stints as a biweekly and weekly. Theshorthorn.com, our online edition, was added in 1997, making Shorthorn content available to anyone, anywhere 24/7. The Shorthorn, which celebrated its centennial in 2019, remains one of UTA’s oldest traditions and most-respected sources of news, information and experience.

Name: Karsh Journalism Fellowship
Description:
The just-launched Karsh Journalism Fellowship is the world’s only journalism program that gives early-career journalists education, training, and mentorship to report on Jewish issues with depth and accuracy.

The fellowship is nonpartisan and adheres to the highest standards of journalism. Its mentors include journalists from The New York Times, Atlantic, New Yorker, CNN and many esteemed outlets. It is open to recent J-school graduates and working journalists on all platforms. 

In the inaugural year, we will select 10 fellows from around the country who will attend a total of three retreats, in Los Angeles, New York and Washington, D.C. Fellows receive a $4,000 stipend and all travel expenses paid.

During the three retreats, fellows will learn from academics, activists, journalists and Jewish leaders. There will be on-site visits, such as to the Academy Museum in L.A. for a session with a leading showrunner on Jews and Hollywood, as well as sessions examining Israel, antisemitism, the Holocaust, the Jewish vote, and other issues.

The fellowship is nonpartisan and dedicated to the highest journalistic standards. The fellows, mentors and presenters will come from a variety of backgrounds, outlooks and platforms. 

Applications now open!

Name: Cowboy Channel
Description:
The Cowboy Channel is the official network of ProRodeo and the first 24-hour television network totally dedicated to western sports and the western lifestyle. Headquartered in the Fort Worth Stockyards, The Cowboy Channel features content focused on ProRodeo, bull riding, roping, reining, barrel racing, and other western sports genres, along with western fashion and music. The lineup also features a wide variety of “live” coverage from major western events showcasing the world’s toughest and most talented cowboys and cowgirls.

On June 19, 2017, Patrick Gottsch, the CEO of Rural Media Group, made an announcement. He revealed that on July 1, FamilyNet would undergo a significant transformation, becoming The Cowboy Channel. This rebranding would shift the network's focus to Western sports and rodeo events, which had proven highly popular on RFD-TV. Gottsch expressed gratitude to Sony Pictures Television for their contribution to the network's success but acknowledged the intense competition in the classic television space. Networks like MeTV, Antenna TV, Cozi TV, Heroes & Icons, and various streaming options had made the landscape fiercely competitive and crowded. Therefore, the idea of a Western sports network was seen as a unique opportunity to stand out in cable and satellite lineups.

The Cowboy Channel's initial programming included encore presentations of events from RFD's The American Rodeo, the Calgary Stampede, and the archives of the Professional Bull Riders. Sony's archived content was subsequently moved to its own GetTV at the beginning of 2018.

In 2020, The Cowboy Channel signed a multi-year agreement with the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association, securing the rights to televise their major events, including the National Finals Rodeo.

Name: The Polis Project, Inc
Description:
The Polis Project, Inc is a New York-based global magazine of dissent that documents communities in resistance at the intersection of politics, art, and culture. We are a hybrid research and journalism organization. Our work documents the rise of authoritarianism and right-wing movements — from Hindutva nationalism in India to far-right governance in Europe, from settler colonialism in Palestine to the criminalization of dissent across the Global Majority. We report on how majoritarian politics weaponizes race, gender, caste, and religion against communities already at the margins. Our work is explicitly feminist, anti-caste, and anti-imperialist.

We are based in New York, but we were built for the world: a publishing infrastructure deliberately built as a platform in exile, enabling work that is no longer possible — or safe at home. The story is our unit of change. We publish long-form journalism, cultural criticism, interviews, podcasts, and photo essays and commission from within the communities we cover, giving authorship to sex workers, queer and trans writers, labor organizers, informal and migrant workers, communities navigating racial, majoritarian and occupation violence, war and genocide, conflict-affected writers, Dalit and caste-oppressed communities, and Indigenous and land-defending peoples.

Name: NABJ CHICAGO CHAPTER

The original name of the organization was the Chicago Association of Black Journalists.

Four Chicago members – Vernon Jarrett, Francis Ward, Paul Delaney and Max Robinson – joined more than a dozen other journalists from across the country to found the National Association of Black Journalists in 1975.

The purpose of the NABJ Chapter is to bring together Chicago-area African-American journalists dedicated to truth and excellence in newsgathering and reporting, and equality in the media industry. To accomplish this mission, the organization seeks to: strengthen the ties between Blacks who work in majority-owned media and Blacks who work in the Black-owned media; assist Black journalists in upgrading their skills for upward mobility toward managerial and supervisory positions; encourage students to identify careers in journalism; and award scholarships to Black journalism students of accredited colleges and universities.

We operate as a multiplatform digital newsroom where local reporting, community features, student-produced media, business profiles, historical pieces, and arts and culture coverage can be published and shared across communities. By collaborating with traditional local newspapers, schools, civic organizations, and individual contributors, we help rural voices reach beyond a single town or county line—strengthening regional connection while respecting local identity.

We do not use paywalls or traditional subscriptions in our digital newsroom model. We believe reliable local information should be freely available so people can stay informed and make decisions that affect their families, businesses, and communities. Instead, our work is supported through sponsorships from local businesses, organizations, and individual supporters who understand the value of strong, independent local media and want to help sustain it.

These sponsorships quite literally keep the lights on. They support reporting, technology, and storytelling that might otherwise disappear in rural areas where traditional news business models are no longer sustainable.  Our sponsors are not buying influence—they are investing in access, visibility, and continuity for the communities they serve.

Preserving local history and community legacy is central to our mission. Local history does not live only in museums or textbooks; it exists in newspapers, school activities, family milestones, business openings, photographs, obituaries, and the everyday moments that define rural life.
